plan.title: When the bottleneck moves: how engineering teams reorganise around agents
plan.thesis: AI raised the volume of code but not the output. The constraint moved from writing to review. The teams that improved delivery without degrading stability moved intent into a verifiable artifact and changed who owns what; teams that only added agents got the volume without the gain.
plan.audience: Engineering leaders and senior engineers deciding how to reorganise delivery with coding agents, 2026-2027

sources.title: METR: measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced developers
sources.org: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein / METR

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: In the randomized controlled trial, experienced open-source developers allowed to use AI tools took 19% longer to complete issues, a significant slowdown.
claims.quote: When developers are allowed to use AI tools, they take 19% longer to complete issues—a significant slowdown that goes against developer beliefs and expert forecasts.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: Developers expected AI to speed them up by 24%, and even after experiencing the slowdown they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%.
claims.quote: This gap between perception and reality is striking: developers expected AI to speed them up by 24%, and even after experiencing the slowdown, they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: The RCT recruited 16 experienced open-source developers, used 246 real issues averaging two hours each, randomized AI use per issue, and paid developers $150/hr.
claims.quote: To directly measure the real-world impact of AI tools on software development, we recruited 16 experienced developers from large open-source repositories (averaging 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines of code) that they’ve contributed to for multiple years. Developers provide lists of real issues (246 total) that would be valuable to the repository—bug fixes, features, and refactors that would normally be part of their regular work. Then, we randomly assign each issue to either allow or disallow use of AI while working on the issue. When AI is allowed, developers can use any tools they choose (primarily Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet—frontier models at the time of the study); when disallowed, they work without generative AI assistance. Developers complete these tasks (which average two hours each) while recording their screens, then self-report the total implementation time they needed. We pay developers $150/hr as compensation for their participation in the study.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: The study ruled out differential issue dropping and found that developers submitted similar quality PRs with and without AI.
claims.quote: We rule out many experimental artifacts—developers used frontier models, complied with their treatment assignment, didn’t differentially drop issues (e.g. dropping hard AI-disallowed issues, reducing the average AI-disallowed difficulty), and submitted similar quality PRs with and without AI.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: The authors argue benchmarks may overestimate model capabilities by measuring only well-scoped, algorithmically scorable tasks, and that anecdotal speed-up estimates can be very inaccurate.
claims.quote: On the other hand, benchmarks may overestimate model capabilities by only measuring performance on well-scoped, algorithmically scorable tasks. And we now have strong evidence that anecdotal reports/estimates of speed-up can be very inaccurate.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: The authors explicitly limit generalizability, saying they do not claim their developers or repositories represent a majority or plurality of software development work.
claims.quote: We do not claim that our developers or repositories represent a majority or plurality of software development work

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: The authors note that their tool setup may not use optimal prompting or scaffolding, and that domain- or repository-specific training could yield positive speedup.
claims.quote: Cursor does not sample many tokens from LLMs, it may not use optimal prompting/scaffolding, and domain/repository-specific training/finetuning/few-shot learning could yield positive speedup

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: The authors suggest AI capabilities may be comparatively lower in settings with very high quality standards or many implicit documentation, testing, and linting requirements.
claims.quote: Our results also suggest that AI capabilities may be comparatively lower in settings with very high quality standards, or with many implicit requirements (e.g. relating to documentation, testing coverage, or linting/formatting) that take humans substantial time to learn.

claims.claim: By April 2026, in one month, Mux had 600+ users including engineers, PMs, and designers, with 335 active and 197 power users; it powered 5,068 merged PRs across 461 repositories and 10 orgs.
claims.quote:
By April 2026 - in one month - Mux had already powered:

*   **600+ users** including engineers, PMs, and designers, with 335 active and 197 power users.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: Mux users had 3.5x more merged PRs per engineer than baseline, with 39.6 versus 11.4.

claims.claim: The authors caveat that Mux users likely skew toward engineers who were already high-output and AI-forward, so they do not claim Mux is the sole cause.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: The bottleneck moved from how fast code could be written to how many things one engineer could orchestrate at once.
claims.quote: The bottleneck had moved. It was no longer how fast we could write code. It was how many things one engineer could orchestrate at once.

claims.question: q4
claims.claim: When code becomes cheap, engineering work shifts upward to scoping problems, designing solutions, reviewing output, and catching edge cases, while implementation becomes the easy part.
claims.quote: When code becomes cheap, the engineer's job changes. The work that matters shifts upward: scoping problems, designing solutions, reviewing output, catching edge cases. The implementation becomes the easy part.

claims.question: q3
claims.claim: A typical workflow has one engineer supervising three or four agents working in parallel, reviewing each agent's output as it finishes, giving feedback, and merging.
claims.quote: One engineer might have three or four agents working in parallel: one implementing an API, one writing integration tests, one fixing a bug, one refactoring a legacy module. The engineer reviews each as it finishes, provides feedback, and merges.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Mux's value is in plugins, skills, and integrations that encode Coinbase shipping practices and repo conventions into reusable commands, including team-specific review automation.

claims.question: q6
claims.claim: Engineers report a qualitative shift toward attempting work they would not have before, including multi-service refactors, batches of bug fixes, features plus test suites, and multi-day efforts becoming single-session workflows.
claims.quote: Beyond the metrics, engineers consistently report a qualitative shift: they attempt work they wouldn't have before. Refactors that touch multiple services, batches of bug fixes, features plus their test suites. Multi-day efforts become single-session workflows.

sources.title: Team Topologies: stewardship of value flow

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: The source says organisations are measuring AI productivity by volume of generated code or content produced by a button click, and calls this trajectory deeply misguided.
claims.quote:
We see a wild rush where organisations measure productivity by "a zillion lines of code" or content generated by a button click.

At Team Topologies, we believe this trajectory is deeply misguided.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: The source says AI systems require clearly defined, long-lived responsibility boundaries and highly constrained, structured context, analogous to managing human cognitive load.
claims.quote: Instead, AI systems require clearly defined, long-lived boundaries of responsibility and highly constrained, structured context. Just as humans work best when their cognitive load is managed, AI agents work best when the context injected into their operating window is strictly defined and focused.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: The source recommends consuming clean interfaces from a platform so that both human teams and AI agents have their cognitive and contextual loads minimised.
claims.quote: By consuming clean interfaces from the platform, both human teams and AI agents have their cognitive and contextual loads minimised, enabling a safe, rapid flow of value.

claims.question: q3
claims.claim: The source says long-lived teams acting as strict stewards of value flow ensure that only the smallest, highest-quality, and most secure changes are promoted.
claims.quote: Long-lived teams acting as strict stewards of their value flow ensure that only the smallest, highest-quality, and most secure changes are promoted.

claims.question: q4
claims.claim: The source argues AI forces teams to move past construction boundaries and establish stewardship boundaries around value flow and human accountability.
claims.quote: AI forces us to move past "construction boundaries" and instead **establish clear boundaries around the stewardship of value flow and human accountability**.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: The source argues code is a liability and that every extra AI-produced line must be tested, maintained, and secured.
claims.quote: In software delivery, code is a liability, not an asset (even if the accountants tell a different story). Every extra line of code produced by an AI is an extra line that must be tested, maintained, and secured.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: The source claims that putting more code live enlarges the security attack surface and that flooding production with unverified, AI-generated code exponentially increases security risks.
claims.quote: The more code an organisation puts live, the larger its security attack surface becomes. Threat actors - whether nation-states or dark web syndicates - are constantly looking for vulnerabilities. Flooding production with unverified, AI-generated code exponentially increases security risks.

claims.question: q6
claims.claim: The source prescribes end-to-end tiny slices for rapid value flow, deployed safely and quality-verified before iteration, rather than large unverified blocks.
claims.quote: The only approach that works effectively for rapid value flow - with or without AI - is breaking work down into end-to-end tiny slices. Instead of building a massive, unverified block of software/content/data and throwing it over the wall, we must build the smallest possible increment, deploy it safely, verify its quality, and iterate.

sources.title: Charity Majors: AI demands more engineering discipline

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: The author asserts that in 2025 code-production economics flipped: generating code became effectively free and instant, and lines of code became disposable and regenerable.
claims.quote: What happened in 2025 was this: **the economics of code production were turned upside down.** Instead of being very hard, time-consuming, and expensive to generate code, it became effectively free and instant. Lines of code went from being treasured, reused, cared for and carefully curated, to being disposable and regenerable, practically overnight.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: The author proposes reviewable architecture diagrams/artifacts as intent carriers, with code regenerated from architecture changes rather than architecture being inferred from code.
claims.quote: Where are the artifacts I can review and discuss to understand how our architecture is evolving? Where are our architecture artifacts, period? claims.question: q3

claims.quote: Lines of code are not the ideal artifact to review

claims.question: q3

claims.question: q6

claims.quote: The share of software engineering teams that work in short, fast feedback loops (the cardinal sign of discipline in my book) is, and always has been, appallingly small. Five percent, maybe? Definitely less than 10%.

sources.title: Will Larson: revised rules of engineering leadership

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: Deploy frequency rose from about ~6 per week to 200-400 per week; headcount doubled; even doubling prior deploys left 20-30x year-over-year growth; the author attributes this to a two-month deployment/run-migration overhaul done 90% by two infrastructure staff.
claims.quote: A year ago, we deployed manually, and deployed ~6 times a week, and now we deploy 200-400 times a week. Our engineering headcount has doubled, but even if we double the prior deploys, we’re still up 20-30x year-over-year. This is due to a complete overhaul of how we deploy and run migrations, and this migration was done over two months and done 90% by two folks on our infrastructure team.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: Daily use of Claude Code or Cursor rose from about 25% in early January to 100% by end February without a top-down mandate; nearly every PR is now written by harnesses at least in the first pass.
claims.quote: The first day of January, about 25% of folks on our team used Claude Code or Cursor every day. By the end of February, 100% did. We did this without any top-down mandate, just by making the tooling good and chatting with non-adopters to remove sources of friction. Pretty much every PR is written by harnesses now, at least in the first pass.

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: First-pass code is nearly free, but working code is not free and its cost depends on the development harness.
claims.quote: While 1st-pass code is nearly free, the cost of working code depends on your development harness, and is not free.

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: Design documents and PRs thrown over the wall to other teams did not go anywhere; slop PRs and design documents are cheap but actively harmful, requiring cleanup and poisoning the LLM context.
claims.quote: Where we’ve tried to throw design documents and PRs “over the wall” to engineers on other teams, they’ve never gone anywhere. Slop pull requests and design documents are cheap, but are actively harmful. They not only have to be cleaned up and repaired, their context poisons the LLM, leading to worse outcomes than starting over.

claims.question: q3
claims.claim: Human base-case code review is slower and less effective than good harness review; harnesses miss things, but so do humans, and most areas are relatively safe while some higher-risk areas are exceptions.
claims.quote: For example, the base case of code review from a human is slower and less effective than a good harness’ code review. Of course, the harness will miss things, but so will human reviewers, and most areas are relatively safe to make changes. Of course, there are some higher risk areas, where this doesn’t hold true.

claims.question: q3
claims.claim: The first pass of code review is done by the same harness that implements the change, with the writing context cleared, so humans can focus on higher-value feedback.
claims.quote: The first pass of code review is done by the same harness that implements the changes, cleared of the context used to write the change, allowing humans to focus on higher value feedback.

claims.question: q4
claims.claim: Quick, good, durable decision-making is a prerequisite to benefit from AI, and the author says the average CTO role has become substantially more technical and less bureaucratic than a year ago.
claims.quote: Your team and company can only benefit from this increased pace of execution if you can make durable decisions quickly, and those decisions are good. This is the primary reason, in my opinion, why the average CTO role has necessarily become substantially more technical and less bureaucratic than a year ago.

sources.title: Simon Willison: parallel coding agents

claims.question: q1
claims.claim: The author identifies code review speed as the natural bottleneck for AI-generated code, especially when agents can churn out changes faster than one person can keep up.
claims.quote: I was pretty skeptical about this at first. AI-generated code needs to be reviewed, which means the natural bottleneck on all of this is how fast I can review the results. claims.question: q2
